subsystems.name: Light emitters
subsystems.role: send near-infrared light through the scalp into the cortex.
parts: LEDs or laser diodes at two wavelengths

subsystems.name: Photodetectors
subsystems.role: measure how much light returns after passing through tissue.

subsystems.name: Optode array and montage
subsystems.role: positions source–detector pairs over a target region, usually the forehead.

subsystems.name: Headset mechanics
subsystems.role: keeps optodes against the scalp through hair without pressing hard enough to cut off blood flow.

subsystems.name: Signal electronics and firmware
subsystems.role: digitises the faint returning signal and strips ambient noise.

subsystems.name: Processing and classification
subsystems.role: converts raw light into haemoglobin changes and then into a focus or stress score.

buildSteps.title: Pick the wavelengths
buildSteps.detail: Two wavelengths are chosen, typically near 760 nm and 850 nm, so the differing absorption of oxygenated and deoxygenated haemoglobin can be separated.

buildSteps.title: Fix the channel geometry
buildSteps.detail: Source–detector separation sets how deep the light samples: short gaps see mostly scalp blood flow, longer ones reach cortical tissue, so both are included.

buildSteps.title: Assemble the emitters
buildSteps.detail: Small LED or laser-diode dies are mounted, encapsulated and wired to drivers that pulse them in sequence so channels do not interfere.

buildSteps.title: Build the detectors
buildSteps.detail: Photodiodes are paired with low-noise amplifiers and recessed behind baffles so room light does not swamp the tiny returning signal.

buildSteps.title: Design the headset
buildSteps.detail: Probes are arranged over the prefrontal cortex following standard scalp landmarks, mounted on a flexible frame that tolerates head movement and hair.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate the electronics
buildSteps.detail: Each channel's dark current, gain and source power are measured so the raw numbers mean the same thing on every device.

buildSteps.title: Write the signal pipeline
buildSteps.detail: Raw intensity is converted to optical density, then to haemoglobin changes; heartbeats, breathing, Mayer waves and motion spikes are filtered out, often using the short channels as a scalp reference.

buildSteps.title: Train and validate the classifier
buildSteps.detail: Volunteers perform tasks of known difficulty while the headset records; models learn to map cortical response to load, and are tested on people who were not in the training set.

buildSteps.title: Ship with honest limits
buildSteps.detail: The device reports an index with confidence bounds, because forehead fNIRS reflects cortical blood flow with a lag of seconds and is easily confused by jaw clenching, talking or sweating.

prerequisites.why: cheap LEDs, laser diodes and photodiodes make a wearable optical sensor possible.

prerequisites.tech: Low-power analog front ends and wireless chips
prerequisites.why: the returning signal is very faint and must be amplified and streamed without drowning in electrical noise.
it converts measured light attenuation into estimates of oxygenated and deoxygenated haemoglobin.
scalp blood flow and heart-rate signals otherwise contaminate the cortical measurement.
prefrontal oxygenation tracks mental effort on average, but varies widely between people and tasks.
consumer-grade accuracy claims need ground truth from harder, more reliable methods across many users.

pathway.milestone: forehead-only headsets sold for attention training and basic biofeedback
pathway.unlocks: a cheap, safe, wearable window on cortical blood flow.

pathway.milestone: whole-head, dry-optode arrays with better hair penetration and short-channel correction
pathway.unlocks: measurement over motor and language regions, not just the forehead.

pathway.milestone: fusion with EEG and other body signals
pathway.unlocks: separating the fast electrical response from the slow blood-flow response, improving load estimates.

pathway.milestone: validated, individually calibrated workload monitoring in training and safety-critical work
pathway.unlocks: practical use where mistakes are costly — if accuracy and comfort improve enough.
